doc.title: Vince Lateano interviewed by Monk Rowe, San Francisco, California, August 8, 2002

title: Learning Latin styles with Cal Tjader and Poncho Sanchez
summary: He got the Tjader job through John Rae, learned Latin playing from Poncho, and explains regional Latin grooves.

story.theme_name: Charlie Parker, Dizzy and the bebop revolution
story.community_name: Charlie Parker: encounters, lore and legacy

blocks.x: Right. What’s it like trying to absorb the Latin end of things? Because I know you’ve worked with Cal Tjader.

With Cal Tjader. Yeah. Well that was a piece of luck because I was thrown in with Poncho Sanchez and a mutual friend of Cal’s and mine was a great musician/drummer/vibist John Rae. And he’d worked with Cal and he’d worked with Vince Guaraldi and Herbie Mann. He lived out here but he was originally from Boston and spent a lot of time in New York, he’d played with Shearing — played vibes with Shearing — a great musician. And he’s gone. And anyway we were good friends and he told me Cal was looking for somebody, “Do you want to do it?” And I said well I’d had a little Latin experience, but I’m a jazz drummer that plays Latin music, I’m not a Latin drummer. But you had to do both with Cal. He used to say it’s like turning a little switch in your mind, you know, you sit down, you play one style of music, he liked jazz, maybe Philly Joe or something, and then as soon as you start playing the other thing it was kind of like a Tito Puente, that was his frame of reference. And so I had a little knowledge going in. I had enough that it was accepted. And then Poncho was there and Poncho would just say “Yeah,” “no,” you know, when we’re playing. You know, “Do that,” “don’t do that.” So he helped me a lot. But like I said I’m still — compared to what’s happening.
If someone says playing merengue as opposed to, I don’t know, a salsa beat, do you know what that means specifically?
Okay. Because there are so many different categories.

I do. There are a lot that I don’t know I’m sure, but I found out that like it’s regional. Of course Afro-Cuban, Cuba. And that big influence, you know, salsa. And then every country has its own groove. And I think the merengue came from Santo Domingo. So if you do a little research you’d find out each country had its way of doing things. Like the Cubans have a carnival, like all those countries, and when they go down the street they play a groove called the comparsa or Mozambique. And the Brazilians of course do samba. And it’s very similar but it’s different. So a little subtle understanding of that kind of thing helps.
